claim: With the auxiliary loss, router scores for selected vs unselected tokens are almost perfectly separated, so the top-k capacity cannot be changed after training (no inference-time budget control).
justification: Qualitative observation about router score separation in trained MoR models; no controlled comparison against another model.
evidence_quote: Specifically, in our MoR models, we observe that when using an auxiliary loss, the router outputs for selected and unselected tokens are almost perfectly separated.

claim: With no ponder penalty, the halting router learns layer-specialized depth: early layers loop minimally, later layers loop more; loop use starts only after validation CE falls to about 3.27.
justification: Observation of training dynamics (per-layer loop counts over training) within the authors' models; not a comparison between architectures.
evidence_quote: The onset of the increase in the number of loops occurs at approximately the same validation cross-entropy value across all loop configurations, around 3.27 ± 0.59

claim: The ponder penalty weight lambda is set to 0, so loop-count patterns are driven only by the LM loss; the paper does not measure compute savings from halting.
justification: Describes a training hyperparameter choice (lambda = 0); no empirical comparison.
evidence_quote: We set λ = 0 for the majority of our experiments, meaning the model receives no explicit incentive to minimize loop iterations.

claim: Ouro's exit gate suffers train-inference mismatch because the backbone is trained only at full depth; TaH2 trains on-policy with the decider's own depth decisions.
justification: Design-level description contrasting how Ouro and TaH2 train their exit mechanisms; no matched empirical comparison in the claim.
evidence_quote: In contrast, Ouro trains at full depth before applying early exit at inference (Zhu et al., 2025), while TaH trains under an oracle policy and uses learned decisions at inference (Fu et al., 2025b).

claim: Average exit depth overstates wall-clock speedup (ragged halting); savings appear only when prefill is compute-bound and memory is not reduced.
justification: Speed benchmark compares full vs skip execution of the same trained CHASE model at matched thresholds; only loop execution differs.
evidence_quote: To isolate backbone packing, full uses the same O(1)-inloops readout policy as skip, so the two differ only in whether deeper loops are executed for exited tokens.

claim: On A5/S5 length generalization at length 128, FPRM keeps high accuracy while scaling compute with length; TRM+conv+ACT drops on A5 and uses more compute on S5.
justification: FPRM and TRM variants are 7M-parameter models trained with shared state-tracking config for 50 epochs; inference capped at same 320 effective layers.
evidence_quote: We show that it outperforms the baselines on Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, ARC-AGI-1, and state-tracking benchmarks A5 and S5 among 7M parameter models.

claim: Compute-accuracy trade-off of fixed-point halting is controlled by step-size decay rate gamma; larger gamma defers halting and buys accuracy with more compute.
justification: Sweeps test-time halting hyperparameters (gamma, patience) of the same trained FPRM under an identical max inference budget.
evidence_quote: In Figure 8, we demonstrate the effect of the step-size decay rate (γ) and maximum patience (P ) from Algorithm 1 on the halting time and performance at test-time.

claim: A training-free per-token convergence exit outperforms a router trained to predict convergence from the same model.
justification: Training-free exit, trained router, and uniform depth are all policies applied to the same frozen backbone.
evidence_quote: All three policies run on the frozen backbone. None of them updates a weight of the language model.

claim: The learned linear router needs essentially full depth and gives no saving.
justification: Router A2 vs convergence exit A1 are post-hoc depth policies on the same frozen backbone.
evidence_quote: All three policies run on the frozen backbone. None of them updates a weight of the language model.

claim: Fixed-prior depth supervision with simple confidence readouts matches or beats jointly trained learned gates; failure stems from the trajectory induced by joint gate training, not gate expressivity.
justification: MANO fixed-prior vs learned-gate models share the same 4-layer backbone, training split, and 40k-step recipe; only the objective differs.
evidence_quote: All MANO models use the same looped Transformer backbone with 4 layers, 4 attention heads, hidden embedding size 512, and maximum recurrent depth T = 6.

claim: On Ouro checkpoints, post-hoc readouts are highly competitive with the pretrained ponder gate, which is not uniformly Pareto-optimal.
justification: Released Ouro checkpoints evaluated as-is; pretrained ponder gate vs post-hoc readouts on the same recurrent trajectories.
evidence_quote: Unlike the MANO experiments, we do not train or modify these models: we evaluate the released checkpoints as-is and compare the pretrained ponder gate against simple post-hoc readouts applied to the recurrent trajectory.

claim: Large KL-to-prior regularisation collapses the learned gate onto a near-fixed-depth operating point.
justification: Beta sweep over learned-gate MANO models sharing backbone, data split, and 40k-step training; only KL strength varies.
evidence_quote: Learned linear-gate models use either a uniform prior or the same geometric priors, and sweep the KL regularization strength β.

claim: Running a lambda-warmup ACT model beyond trained depth improves accuracy, with a sweet spot around 2x training depth and graceful degradation after.
justification: Same trained lambda-warmup ACT model run for more ponder steps at inference than trained; no retraining or architecture comparison.
evidence_quote: Extended inference (64 steps, trained on 18). The lambda-warmup model peaks at step 36 (66% EM, +14pp over step 17) then gradually degrades but never crashes (64% at step 63).

claim: Fixed-loop looped models collapse when evaluated off their training depth, which motivates elastic training.
justification: Motivational statement citing prior work (Bae et al., Fan et al.); not an experiment in this paper.
evidence_quote: Once trained, their representations collapse when evaluated at shorter or longer depths, since those settings are off-distribution Bae et al. (2024); Fan et al. (2024).

claim: Average depth 1.07 iterations per token gives FLOPs and memory access within 4-5% of the standard model (a FLOP/memory proxy), but measured batch-1 decode latency is still higher than Standard (301.4 s vs 210.6 s), though 2.48x faster than AlwaysThink.
justification: TaH, Standard, AlwaysThink fine-tuned from same Qwen3 backbone on same Open-R1 100K data under equal parameter budgets; latency measured, not matched.
evidence_quote: All models are trained on the balanced Open-R1 (Hugging Face, 2025) mixture (math, QA, and code; 100K samples) using supervised fine-tuning.

claim: Using an on-policy (dynamically recomputed) oracle during backbone training causes training collapse; a static oracle from a separate SFT model is required to break the policy/backbone circular dependency.
justification: Table 4 ablation on TaH-0.6B varies only the oracle iteration policy; backbone, data, and recipe fixed.
evidence_quote: Ablation study on design choices of TaH-0.6B. Each row varies one aspect from the TaH configuration

claim: Per-token early exit can paradoxically reduce throughput in batched inference because of synchronization and missing-KV bottlenecks; parameter sharing mitigates this via continuous depth-wise batching.
justification: Abstract-level motivating statement about early-exit system bottlenecks; not a specific controlled comparison.
evidence_quote: While adaptive computation methods like early-exiting promise to reduce these costs, they introduce a fundamental conflict: the per-token dynamism intended to save computation often creates system-level bottlenecks that can paradoxically reduce throughput in batched inference.

claim: Standard weighted CE over intermediate loop outputs overemphasizes intermediate representations; an aggressive (small) coefficient on intermediate losses plus self-distillation from the final loop works best.
justification: Ablation of early-exit loss strategies on the same recursive Gemma model, each post-trained on 15B tokens.
evidence_quote: Early-exit training utilized 15 billion tokens, either overlapping with uptraining data or entirely new.

claim: Selection ratios trained at fixed values can be changed at inference: raising them lowers PPL, lowering them to 50% keeps PPL near the training config.
justification: Same trained ITT model evaluated with different inference-time token selection ratios versus its training configuration.
evidence_quote: As seen in Table 2, with 4-step thinking and 70% token participation during training, we can flexibly adjust token selections to enhance performance

claim: Reviewing 20% of tokens costs about 6% extra FLOPs (analytic estimate), and measured batch-1 throughput on H100 is 91.6-93.1% of the vanilla model.
justification: Qwen3-30B-A3B SFT vs same model with DND SFT; DND adds only 0.03M parameters. FLOP overhead is analytic, throughput measured.
evidence_quote: Crucially, these substantial performance gains are realized with a negligible increase of only 0.03M parameters, highlighting DND as a highly parameter-efficient approach for unlocking significant capabilities in LLMs.

claim: Sigmoid threshold routers saturate when the target selection ratio is extreme, losing discrimination near the threshold; an explicit distribution-preservation loss is needed.
justification: Design rationale for the Distribution Preservation Loss (sigmoid saturation argument); no controlled comparison stated for this claim.
evidence_quote: This issue is particularly pronounced when the target selection ratio is low (e.g., 20%) or high (e.g., 80%), as the model may push many scores into the sigmoid’s saturation regions.

claim: Token-level halting in UT gives no compute saving until every position halts, while risking some positions halting too early and freezing their memory.
justification: Limitations-section argument about token-level halting; conceptual, not an empirical comparison.
evidence_quote: the token-level halt can limit the writable memory (each position can also be considered as a memory slot with read-write capacities) by halting certain positions too early but without providing any computational saving in return

claim: Replacing GUT's global halt with token-level halting, or removing gating or transition information, severely harms near-IID ListOps accuracy; none of the variants fixes OOD generalization.
justification: GUT ablations trained on the same ListOps split with shared hyperparameters; removing gating changes parameter count, so not iso_param.
evidence_quote: We also keep the same hyperparameters for UT, and GUT as Transformers where possible.

claim: With dynamic halting, GUT training runtime saturates near 5 minutes per epoch as the layer upper bound grows to 30-40, while fixed upper-bound variants grow proportionally; at low bounds a no-halt model can be faster because halting computation adds per-layer cost.
justification: Training runtime per ListOps epoch compared across GUT variants at equal layer upper bounds; variants differ in halting computation, parameter equality not stated.
evidence_quote: We compare the diﬀerent models under diﬀerent upperbound layers (10, 20, 30, and 40).

claim: The ACT-style late-halting penalty requires difficult tuning; beta was tuned on validation and set to 0.1 (0 for Logical Inference).
justification: Describes hyperparameter tuning of the ACT penalty weight; no empirical comparison.
evidence_quote: We tune the β for UT based on validation accuracy on ListOps in [1, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001] and set the value as 0.1.

claim: The Q-exit threshold trades underthinking against overthinking: q = 0.5 is best; larger q often forces all 12 layers and lowers accuracy, smaller q speeds up but underthinks.
justification: Same trained PALBERT models evaluated with different Q-exit thresholds q at inference.
evidence_quote: To do so, we evaluated trained PALBERT models from the ablation study (see Section 4.1) on dev splits of tasks with different values of q.

claim: Results depend strongly on the geometric prior over exit layers, which the authors name as the main limitation; at the best RTE prior the model mostly exits at the last layer.
justification: PALBERT models retrained with different prior lambda under the same ALBERT-Base setup and task data; only the prior varies.
evidence_quote: We followed the experimental setup from the previous sections and trained models with λ ∈ [0.1, 0.15, 0.25, 0.5].

claim: Naive looping fails: performance saturates and declines beyond training depth while spatial position information erodes; this motivates deep supervision and attention modulation.
justification: Naive looped MMDiT evaluated at increasing inference loop depth plus per-loop probing of the same checkpoint.
evidence_quote: Increasing inference loop depth beyond that used in training initially improves performance, then saturates and degrades.

claim: Looping and textual CoT prompt rewriting are complementary: looping helps constraint-resolution subtasks, CoT helps inferring implied content.
justification: Table 3 baseline is 'the non-looped model', defined in Sec. 3 as the same architecture trained without looping on the shared data/recipe.
evidence_quote: We consider two nonlooped baselines, one using the same checkpoint with looping disabled, thereby holding the learned weights and training history fixed, and the other using the same architecture trained without looping.

claim: Test-time recurrence scaling: LIBERO average success rises log-linearly with iterations and saturates around 8-12.
justification: Single trained RD-VLA evaluated with fixed recurrent iteration counts 1 to 32 at test time.
evidence_quote: We first establish the relationship between computational depth and task success rates by evaluating RD-VLA with a fixed number of recurrent iterations Ninf ∈ {1, . . . , 32} on all task suites of LIBERO.

claim: KL-based adaptive stopping matches fixed-depth peak with 34% fewer iterations.
justification: KL-based adaptive stopping vs fixed iteration counts are inference-time strategies on the same RD-VLA model.
evidence_quote: At inference, RD-VLA dynamically allocates compute using an adaptive stopping criterion based on latent convergence.

claim: Depth generalization is bounded: beyond an optimal iteration count, recurrence can saturate or degrade.
justification: Limitation drawn from varying test-time recurrence of the same trained model; no architecture comparison.
evidence_quote: While performance scales predictably with the number of recurrent steps up to some optimal number of iterations, extending recurrence beyond this number of iterations may lead to state saturation or performance degradation rather than continued refinement.

claim: Finite unrolled weight-tied models outperform DEQ variants and similarly structured explicit models in accuracy and time.
justification: Weight-tied vs DEQ share identical parameter space and hyperparameters on CIFAR-10; vs explicit models the weight-tied net has equal depth.
evidence_quote: Note that there exists no difference between the weight-tied model and the DEQ model from the view of parameter space, though the former needs to specify the depth of the tied layer.

claim: Compute allocation is structured: loops increase with remaining pushes and future optimal pushes become linearly decodable over loops.
justification: Analysis of loop allocation and probe decodability within one trained Looped Actor; not a model comparison.
evidence_quote: For the Boxoban environment, we find that the computation allocation is structured: the number of loops increases with the number of remaining pushes and future optimal pushes become increasingly predictable from the latent state over successive loops.

claim: Single-path depth helps then saturates: K from 1 to 5 raises CALVIN 5-step success 82.5 to 88.9; K=7 adds only 0.2.
justification: Table V varies inference depth K on one shared checkpoint per benchmark without retraining.
evidence_quote: Table V compares success and latency using one checkpoint per benchmark setting, varying inference budgets without retraining.

claim: At equal latency, spending compute on width (parallel hypotheses) beats extra single-path depth.
justification: Width vs depth inference configurations evaluated on the same checkpoint; comparison is at equal measured latency, not a different model.
evidence_quote: Within each benchmark setting, all latent configurations in Table V share one checkpoint.

claim: Authors state that no baseline jointly matched for parameters and compute was run.
justification: Authors' limitation statement that no jointly parameter- and compute-matched baseline was run; not itself a comparison.
evidence_quote: Component ablations also do not replace a baseline jointly matched for parameters and compute.

claim: HRM trained only with RL reaches the goal in about 99% of episodes in both dynamic maze environments.
justification: Reports absolute goal-reaching rate of HRM-Agent; no baseline comparison in the claim.
evidence_quote: The HRM-Agent model is able to reach the goal in approximately 99% of all episodes in both environments.

claim: Authors acknowledge selective disclosure; no non-looped matched baseline or loop ablation is reported in this version.
justification: Authors' statement about selective disclosure; describes reporting scope, not an empirical comparison.
evidence_quote: While the present paper already provides strong evidence for the effectiveness of LoopWM, the current manuscript is intentionally selective in disclosure scope.

claim: Test-time loop count trades accuracy for speed; peak at K=8, no gain from deeper inference, K=4 (outside training range) still works.
justification: Same trained LoopTrack evaluated at different test-time loop counts K, including outside training range, without retraining.
evidence_quote: Despite lying outside the training range [6, 12], K = 4 still achieves 67.8 SUC at 151 FPS without retraining, demonstrating generalization to unseen inference depths.

claim: A pretrained MDLM can be converted to a fixed-point model with 4% of pretraining steps and beat the 1M-step FP-MDLM.
justification: Adapted FP-MDLM vs from-scratch FP-MDLM compared at equal sampling budgets (transformer-block forward passes); training histories differ, so training not matched.
evidence_quote: We compare the generative perplexity and unigram entropy of base FP-MDLM and adapted FP-MDLM across different budgets.

claim: Running more model cycles than trained collapses performance (no test-time extrapolation).
justification: Same trained H2L3 LoopVL model run with more H cycles at inference, reusing parameters without retraining.
evidence_quote: Table 4 fixes the trained H2L3 model and changes only the H/L configuration used at inference.

claim: Recursive refinement drives control cost down by over 90% from iteration 0 to 3 on the nonlinear oscillator, reaching the SQP-optimal mean cost.
justification: Cost reduction across refinement iterations 0 to 3 of the same trained TRC; SQP is a reference optimum, not a model baseline.
evidence_quote: Cost reduction exceeds 90% from iteration 0 to 3.

claim: TRM-style dual-latent recursion is parameter- and FLOP-expensive without matching accuracy; depth-conditioned recursion (depth injected as input, per-step loss) gives the best accuracy-per-parameter/FLOP.
justification: Seven surrogate configurations evaluated on the same datasets; parameters and FLOPs deliberately vary and are compared via Pareto frontiers, not matched.
evidence_quote: To thoroughly evaluate the tracking and retrieval performance, we compare our approach against seven baseline configurations categorized across four distinct architectural paradigms:

claim: Position-supervised recursive refinement reduces median terminal error from 21.7 km to 0.027 km on single-rev LEO with a 2.3M model.
justification: Error reduction is relative to the uncorrected Keplerian Lambert input that the same model refines (refinement output vs its own initial guess).
evidence_quote: All three variants reduce the terminal error relative to the uncorrected Keplerian Lambert baseline, but the refinement-based variants are more accurate by two orders of magnitude.

claim: Shared iterative refinement with adaptive exit and routed adapters cuts parameters 70.4% and average compute 51.3% relative to MP-SENet while reaching WB-PESQ 3.37.
justification: ADER and MP-SENet baselines trained on VCTK-DEMAND with the same 100-epoch recipe; parameters and compute deliberately differ.
evidence_quote: All models are trained for 100 epochs using AdamW with a learning rate of 5 × 10−4 , β1 = 0.8, β2 = 0.99, with a global batch size of 4.

claim: Reconstruction improves monotonically over thought ticks in a preliminary study.
justification: Reconstruction quality tracked across thought ticks T=0..4 of the same trained ThinkSR model.
evidence_quote: Preliminary experiments under a fixed four-tick training horizon reveal a progressive reconstruction trajectory.

claim: Loop extrapolation: inference with S=24 (> Smax=12) keeps improving NLL; S=1 underperforms the baseline.
justification: S=24 vs training max is same-model loop extrapolation; S=1 vs MDM baseline is matched in parameters, training data, and total training FLOPs.
evidence_quote: We train two models, LoopMDM and a non-looped MDM baseline, matched in parameter count, training data, and total training FLOPs, differing only in per-step training and inference compute, which are controlled by the loop count S.

claim: A hidden-state-change stopping rule reduces average loops from 12 to about 5 while preserving most gains.
justification: Hidden-state-change stopping vs fixed S=12 are inference-time loop policies on the same LoopMDM checkpoint.
evidence_quote: At this operating point, adaptive looping reduces the average number of iterations to roughly half of that for a fixed S = 12 while maintaining comparable zero-shot and generative perplexity.

claim: Loop extrapolation depends on residual scaling: alpha=1 degrades at high loop counts, while 1/L-type scaling extrapolates beyond the pretraining limit; the deployed model works at about twice the mean training loops.
justification: Residual-scaling variants share architecture and continued-pretraining recipe; extrapolation and 2x-loop deployment evaluate each model at varied inference loop counts.
evidence_quote: We continue pretraining for our looped models with different values of α for 10,000 more steps in the Stage 2 setting to enable longer-context processing.

claim: Loop placement matters: looping L9-11 beats L15-17 on understanding and reasoning; L3-5 harms transcription.
justification: Placement variants loop a 3-layer block of the same 28-layer Qwen2.5-Omni Thinker, so unique parameters are equal; training details for variants not reported.
evidence_quote: We build on the 28-layer Qwen2.5-Omni-7B Thinker [13] and select the recurrent block and response readout boundary through placement experiments.

claim: Adaptive (sufficiency-based) exit selection beats any fixed exit iteration, and optimal depth varies by task suite.
justification: Adaptive vs fixed exit iterations evaluated on the same (3 x 8) trained LoopVLA at inference.
evidence_quote: Under a fixed (3 ⊗ 8) configuration, we evaluate different inference layer selections (Table 5).

claim: Gating is needed: recurrent ResNet blocks do not get the compute benefit, and TRM-style deep recursion works worse.
justification: Recurrent block types swapped with identical RL hyperparameters and recurrent steps; parameter counts differ (LSTM has twice IRU's).
evidence_quote: Only the architecture relevant code is changed when comparing IRU, MLP or ResNets.

claim: Weight reuse does not reduce execution cost: the looped CNN uses more MACs and higher latency than a Flux-style reference.
justification: Untrained architectural profiling against a local Flux-style CNN reference; neither parameters nor compute nor accuracy are matched.
evidence_quote: This is an architectural benchmark, not an accuracy-matched comparison of pretrained checkpoints.

claim: Small feature updates in a trained pass still matter a lot (bypass loses ~7.8 dB), and truncation produces output-range errors, so the recurrence is not an any-time decoder.
justification: Bypass and truncation interventions applied to passes of the same trained LoopVAE checkpoint.
evidence_quote: Shared weights do not imply equivalent loop positions. All 224 separately applied single-pass bypasses reduce PSNR relative to their image’s full schedule.

claim: Test-time cycles beyond training (up to 7 vs 3) monotonically increase Dice and saturate ('prediction convergence').
justification: Same trained RecycleNet evaluated with more recycling cycles at inference (up to 7) than its training maximum of 3.
evidence_quote: During inference, we increase the number of cycles to a maximum of 7 cycles to benefit from the property discussed in Section 4.4 and always report metrics using the maximum number of cycles.

claim: A third pass gives only marginal pooled gains and slightly worse macro EER; adaptive halting matches two passes at 1.18 average passes.
justification: Fixed two-pass, three-pass, and adaptive halting are inference modes of one CoReLoop model trained with all-depth supervision.
evidence_quote: The second term minimizes classification loss under the induced exit distribution, helping mitigate the mismatch between all-depth supervision during training and sequential halting at inference.

claim: Deep supervision with detached rounds lets inference depth extend past the training depth with small gains on 3 of 4 datasets (MicroLens saturates near 4 and declines).
justification: Same trained RecRec evaluated at inference depths beyond training depth N = 9.
evidence_quote: Deep supervision enables RecRec to use flexible reasoning depth at inference.

claim: The heterogeneous design remains competitive with 10.8% fewer downstream parameters than the matched baseline.
justification: All variants trained only on ASVspoof 2019 LA with shared recipe; heterogeneous model has 10.8% fewer parameters, so not iso_param.
evidence_quote: All models are trained exclusively on the ASVspoof 2019 Logical Access (19LA) training set, with model selection performed on its development set.

claim: Weight sharing in space and depth regularizes the model so it learns with far fewer free parameters from 28k samples.
justification: CNN baselines are results from prior works trained on the same task; parameter counts differ by about 8x.
evidence_quote: and some state-of-the-art convolutional models — ResNet18, ResNet50, CorNet-S and DenseNet121 — trained on the same task in [3,21,22].

claim: Feedback connections iteratively refine the representation until a stable prediction; the hybrid CNN+Transformer and feedback are both important per ablation.
justification: Table 3 ablation variants (Conv. ViT, Conv. RViT, steerable CNN) all trained on the 28k-image regime; parameter equality not stated.
evidence_quote: Following, we report some in-depth analysis of the RViTs performed with 28k training images.

claim: Feature quality keeps improving over recursion iterations (decoded intermediate features).
justification: Intermediate features of the same trained ucell-768 decoded at different recursion iterations.
evidence_quote: Feature outputs from the T module of ucell were incepted at various specific iterations and were evaluated by projecting to output space using the head (H) module and compared with the ground truth label.

claim: Across passes the shared block resolves constraints in a fixed order: brackets, rings, then valence.
justification: Mechanistic observation (error classes and linear probes across passes) within one trained model; not a model comparison.
evidence_quote: We find here a fixed hierarchy of increasing scope. The shared block resolves brackets by pass 2 (local pairings within a few tokens), rings by pass 4 (long-range digit pairing across tens of tokens), and valence by pass 8

claim: More supervision steps overfit and latent depth beyond 3 gives diminishing returns.
justification: ViTRM supervision-depth and latent-depth variants trained on CIFAR-10 with other factors held constant; recursion depth does not change parameters.
evidence_quote: We investigate the effect of supervision depth Nsupervision on model performance by varying this hyperparameter across values {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} while holding other factors constant.

claim: More fixed recurrent steps improve occluded-input accuracy (saturating at 4-5), and dynamic halting beats fixed T=5.
justification: Table 3(c) varies fixed recurrent steps during inference on the trained PRISM and compares to its dynamic halting.
evidence_quote: Dynamic halting achieves 44.6 on PatchMask0.8 and 69.2 on OnlyOne112, outperforming fixed-step inference (T =5), demonstrating its ability to adapt computation to input difficulty for improved robustness and efficiency.

claim: Halting step count barely changes clean accuracy but matters under occlusion; the model uses more steps for harder (occluded) inputs.
justification: Max halting steps varied during training (same architecture, ImageNet-1K); step-allocation under occlusion is inference-time analysis of one model.
evidence_quote: Model Variants Clean PatchMask0.8 BlockMask112 OnlyOne112 (a) Max halting steps during training 4 5 6

claim: Each recurrent iteration refines 2D tokens, updates 1D latents and adds capacity, giving variable-length tokenization from 32 to 256 tokens.
justification: Method description of the recurrent tokenizer's per-iteration behavior; fulltext unavailable locally, decision based on claim content.

claim: Token count aligns with image entropy, familiarity and downstream needs.
justification: Observation that one tokenizer's token count tracks image properties; no architecture comparison. Fulltext unavailable locally.

claim: Returns diminish beyond r=32 (91.57% -> 91.27% at r=64).
justification: Hierarchical model (trained with mean recurrence 32) evaluated across test-time recurrence steps r; r=32 vs r=64 is same model.
evidence_quote: Figure 4 illustrates the performance scaling of three model variants across varying recurrence steps r

claim: The recurrence is not a fixed-point iteration: state norm grows while direction converges to the endpoint.
justification: Analysis of latent-state dynamics (norm growth, direction convergence) within one trained model.
evidence_quote: Unlike deep equilibrium networks [Bai et al., 2019], our recurrence does not converge to a fixed point in feature space. Instead, the state norm ∥zk ∥ grows monotonically with k.

claim: Inference with more loops than training (T=10-16 vs 8) is stable, attributed to the LTI-stable injection.
justification: Same RD-ViT trained at T=8 evaluated with fewer and more loop iterations at inference.
evidence_quote: The model was trained with T=8 loop iterations (red dashed line). At inference time, Dice increases from 0.61 (T=2) to 0.77 (T=6) and saturates.

claim: Random initial state plus injection of the embedded input at every step stabilizes recurrence and promotes path independence; injecting only at the start would not be stable.
justification: Architectural design rationale citing prior deep-thinking literature; no experiment reported for this claim.
evidence_quote: This architecture is based on deep thinking literature, where it is shown that injecting the latent inputs e in every step (Bansal et al., 2022)

claim: Additive injection works for small models but concatenation works best at scale; a timestep-conditioned core harms extrapolation; added diffusion-style noise did not help.
justification: Reports outcomes of preliminary design ablations (addition vs concatenation, noise, step-conditioning) without describing their models, data, or compute.
evidence_quote: We ran several ablations with iterative schemes even more similar to diffusion models, such as si = R(e, si−1 ) + n where n ∼ N (0, σi In·h ), but find the injection of noise not to help in our preliminary experiments

claim: A core block conditioned on the step index breaks path independence and extrapolation.
justification: Step-conditioned core result comes from unreported preliminary ablations; baseline and matching unspecified.
evidence_quote: We also evaluated and si = Ri (e, si−1 ), i.e. a core block that takes the current step as input (Peebles and Xie, 2023), but find that this interacts badly with path independence, leading to models that cannot extrapolate.

claim: At scale, the first runs (parameter-free norms, no embedding scale, additive adapter) collapsed: the model learned to ignore the recurrence, so perplexity was the same at 1 or 32 iterations.
justification: The failed run's single checkpoint shows equal validation perplexity at 1 and 32 recurrences; same model, different loop counts.
evidence_quote: However, we quickly find that this training run is not able to leverage test-time compute effectively (right plot), as validation perplexity is the same whether 1 or 32 recurrences are used.

claim: Training and inference need only constant memory regardless of effective depth, because gradients are computed by implicit differentiation at the equilibrium.
justification: Methodological property of implicit differentiation (constant memory); not a matched empirical comparison.
evidence_quote: Using this approach, training and prediction in these networks require only constant memory, regardless of the effective “depth” of the network.

claim: Stacking several DEQs gives no extra representational power over a single DEQ.
justification: Theoretical result (Theorem 2, universality of single-layer DEQs).
evidence_quote: The theorem essentially shows that stacking multiple DEQs does not create extra representational power over a single DEQ.

claim: Weight-tied deep sequence models tend to converge to a fixed point as depth grows, motivating solving for the equilibrium directly.
justification: Qualitative hypothesis and observation motivating the DEQ formulation; not a comparison between models.
evidence_quote: we hypothesize and observe that such weight-tied models tend to converge to a fixed point as depth increases towards infinity (see Appendix D for empirical evidence).

claim: ACT lets a recurrent network learn how many computation steps to take per input, deterministically and differentiably.
justification: Description of the ACT mechanism's properties; not an empirical comparison.
evidence_quote: ACT requires minimal changes to the network architecture, is deterministic and differentiable, and does not add any noise to the parameter gradients.

claim: Behaviour is sensitive to the hand-chosen time penalty tau.
justification: Sensitivity observed across networks of the same architecture trained on the same task with a grid of time penalties tau.
evidence_quote: A logarithmic grid search over time penalties was performed for each experiment, with 20 randomly initialised networks trained for each value of τ .

claim: Restricting recursion to shallow efficient-attention layers avoids the KV-cache growth and overhead of whole-network looping as in the Universal Transformer.
justification: Architectural design argument contrasting YOCO-U with the Universal Transformer; no empirical comparison in this claim.
evidence_quote: While UT applies recursive computation to the entire network, leading to redundant overhead and potential optimization difficulties, YOCO-U restricts the recursion to the shallow self-decoder modules.

claim: The authors lack a non-looped control at equal parameters and compute, because the matching non-looped shape changes the active-expert share.
justification: Authors' limitation statement about a missing equal-parameter, equal-compute non-looped control; not itself a comparison.
evidence_quote: First, we have no non-looped control at equal parameters and compute: the non-looped model with the expert parameters and expert calls of (8, 8, 2) is (4, 16, 1)

claim: Re-injecting the prelude output at every step (Huginn/Parcae-style) suppresses iteration-to-iteration differentiation; LoopMoE removes it and uses pure recursion from h_pre.
justification: Design rationale for removing prelude re-injection; no ablation isolating re-injection is reported for this claim.
evidence_quote: re-inject the prefix output hpre additively at every step, requiring an ill-defined h0 at the first iteration and allowing a constant hpre to dominate the residual stream, thereby suppressing iteration-toiteration differentiation.

claim: Dense loops cannot be matched to a non-looped baseline on both parameters and FLOPs; MoE makes this possible.
justification: Conceptual argument that dense loops couple parameters and FLOPs; not an empirical comparison.
evidence_quote: Iterating a dense block multiplies compute without altering parameters, which makes it impossible to simultaneously match a non-looped baseline on both axes.

claim: A pre-transformer, looped transformer and post-transformer structure, mirroring preprocessing, iterative optimization and postprocessing, gives algorithmic inductive bias.
justification: Description of the AlgoFormer architecture and its intended inductive bias.
evidence_quote: our transformer framework consists of a pre-transformer that is responsible for task preprocessing, a looped transformer for iterative optimization algorithms, and a post-transformer for producing the desired results after post-processing.

claim: Without input injection a path-independent network would forget the input, so any model that fits the data must be path dependent.
justification: Theoretical argument about path independence and input injection.
evidence_quote: Without input injection, a PI network would necessarily forget the input; hence, any model which successfully fits the training distribution must be path dependent.

claim: Base CoTFormer perplexity results reproduce exactly within confidence intervals.
justification: Reproduced CoTFormer (same configurations, single seed) compared to the original paper's published 3-seed numbers.
evidence_quote: Theirs are the original results, reported with Standard Error of the Mean (SEM) over 3 seeds. Ours represents a single-seed evaluation showing per-batch 95% confidence intervals.

claim: Halting marginally hurt MT; the best MT model uses no ACT.
justification: ACT-vs-no-ACT MT result stated only in the introduction; no table, run description, or matching details for the ACT MT model.
evidence_quote: such a conditional computation mechanism can in fact improve accuracy on several smaller, structured algorithmic and linguistic inference tasks (although it marginally degraded results on MT).

claim: Continuous depth-wise batching with early exiting gives up to 2.66x simulated generation speedup over vanilla models, but this rests on oracle exits and hypothetical throughput.
justification: Simulated throughput of recursive models (half the layers looped twice) vs full-size vanilla models of the same depth, using oracle exits and dummy weights.
evidence_quote: For example, Gemma 2B (Team et al., 2024) with 18 layers can be converted to a recursive variant with 2 blocks by storing weights for only the first 9 layers.

claim: Progressive denoising is unnecessary at inference; constant maximal noise is best, and removing noise collapses performance.
justification: Same trained model run with different inference-time noise schedules (fixed maximal, annealed, no noise).
evidence_quote: Meanwhile, performing inference on the same model with annealed noise yields a reduced performance of 99.56%.

claim: Training the looped architecture from scratch performs significantly better than upcycling a pretrained standard Transformer into a looped one (no numbers reported).
justification: From-scratch vs upcycled looped training compared without reported numbers, data, or compute details.
evidence_quote: We compare this approach against training the looped architecture from scratch.

claim: Two passes give the best trade-off, retaining about 75% of a standard Transformer's token efficiency; more passes add little, slow training and destabilize optimization.
justification: Pass-count variants reuse the same shared layer stack, so unique parameters are equal; data and compute settings not reported.
evidence_quote: It increases the effective computational depth and model capacity without introducing another set of parameters.

claim: Sharing the KV cache across loop passes halves KV memory but consistently yields lower gains than the full non-sharing loop, so it was not used.
justification: KV-sharing and non-sharing loop variants use the same looped stack (sharing adds no parameters); data and compute details not reported.
evidence_quote: Although the sharing configuration reduces the KV-cache by half, its performance gains are consistently lower than those of the full, non-sharing loop configuration.

claim: AdRNNs zero-shot generalize to harder unseen difficulty levels by increasing recurrent iterations at test time.
justification: Trained AdRNNs evaluated on harder unseen difficulty levels, adaptively using more recurrent steps at test time than in training.
evidence_quote: Notably, AdRNNs trained with ACT choose to make thalt during inference on longer mazes greater than thalt used on the shorter training mazes.

claim: Looped transformers whose middle layers repeat Theta(log n) times can recognize regular languages and solve graph connectivity, which fixed-depth transformers cannot under standard conjectures.
justification: Theoretical expressivity result (Theorems 1-2).
evidence_quote: We prove that even such highly uniform transformers, when allowed log-depth, can recognize regular languages2 and solve graph connectivity, two important reasoning problems known to be beyond fixed-depth transformers

claim: Scaling depth is more efficient than scaling width (superpolynomial) or CoT steps (superlogarithmic) for these problems.
justification: Theoretical comparison of depth vs width vs CoT scaling (Theorems 3-4).
evidence_quote: Further, we showed that scaling depth to solve these problems is more efficient than scaling width (which requires superpolynomial increase) or scaling chain-of-thought steps (which requires superlogarithmic increase).

claim: Log depth cannot solve P-complete problems unless NC = P.
justification: Complexity-theoretic limitation conditional on NC != P; not empirical.
evidence_quote: Unless NC = P, log-depth (or even polylog-depth) transformers cannot express P-complete problems including solving linear equalities

claim: An implicit weight-tied refinement block improves Mask R-CNN mask AP by about 1% with 30% of the mask-head parameters.
justification: Mask R-CNN with and without IFR trained on COCO with the same 1x schedule; mask-head parameters differ (IFR uses 30%).
evidence_quote: Performance comparison between four 3 × 3 convs and our IFR on two-stage instance segmentation frameworks, evaluated on COCO val2017 set. 1x (12 epochs) training strategy is adopted.

claim: The latency advantage relies on decoding being memory-bound; extra loop FLOPs are hidden, not removed.
justification: Mechanistic explanation of PLT latency (memory-bound decoding hides extra FLOPs); not a matched comparison.
evidence_quote: Compared with a standard non-loop decoder, it adds FLOPs that improve accuracy, yet the latency increase is negligible because decoding is memory-bound [44].

claim: The sampler does not reduce FLOPs; speedup comes from exploiting GPU parallelism in memory-bound decoding (FLOPs are actually higher than AR per token).
justification: Description of where the sampler's speedup comes from; not an empirical comparison.
evidence_quote: While this approach does not reduce FLOPs, it effectively exploits modern GPU architectures by unlocking additional opportunities for parallelization.

claim: Huginn-0125 supports cross-recurrence KV sharing (cache of latest recurrence only) matching baseline GSM8K accuracy with r-times less KV memory.
justification: KV-sharing policy applied to the same trained Huginn-0125 checkpoint versus its default cache.
evidence_quote: As shown in Figure 3, the trained Huginn-0125 model inherently supports KV cache sharing, allowing us to store only the KV state of the most recent recurrence for each token position

claim: Diffusion sampler beats tuned self-speculative decoding (which itself is about 1.9x over static AR on GSM8K).
justification: Diffusion-forcing sampler vs speculative decoding vs static AR are decoding methods applied to the same model.
evidence_quote: Show that diffusion forcing sampling outperforms even well-tuned speculative decoding baselines for the same model with speed gains that can be smoothly traded off against accuracy.

claim: Requirements for the sampler: input injection and intermediate states decodable to approximately correct outputs; models trained with a fixed recurrence count may fail.
justification: States prerequisites for the sampler (input injection, decodable intermediate states); not an empirical comparison.
evidence_quote: While this property is generally satisfied, it may fail in models trained exclusively with a fixed number of recurrences r, where decoding from earlier steps can yield nonsensical outputs rather than approximate versions of the intended result.

claim: Shared cache saves memory not time: at equal batch LPT is 3-8% slower than LT, and looped decoding at batch 1 is 2.3-5.7x slower than STD.
justification: LPT, LT, and STD are parameter-matched and trained on the same FineWeb-Edu tokens with the same seed and data order; speed measured, compute not matched.
evidence_quote: All our comparisons are parameter-matched, including DEEPSTD, and we do not train a standard Transformer matched in decoding FLOPs instead, which at five recursions would have several times the parameters.

claim: Throughput gains come only through larger batches: LPT peak throughput 7-91% above LT.
justification: LPT vs LT throughput: parameter-matched models with equal recursions, trained on the same data with identical seed and data order.
evidence_quote: The main tables report one run per configuration, with the same initialization seed and data order across models.

claim: Untrained first-recursion-only KV reuse hurts Ouro, so the benefit of sharing requires training it in; the paper argues sharing is an inductive bias, not just a cost.
justification: Cites Ouro's own finding: KV-cache policies applied to the released Ouro checkpoint without retraining; inductive-bias point is interpretation.
evidence_quote: Without retraining, Huginn (Geiping et al., 2025) reuses caches cyclically with little quality loss, and Ouro (Zhu et al., 2025) can keep only the final or an averaged cache.

claim: Quantizing cross-loop KV residuals is more accurate than quantizing full KV per loop (KIVI4 per-loop gives larger drop).
justification: Residual vs per-loop KV quantization are training-free inference compressions on the same pretrained looped model.
evidence_quote: To reduce these structural redundancies, we propose FlashLoop, a training-free and loop-native inference framework for pretrained looped Transformers.

claim: Savings grow with context length and loop count; at 32K, KV storage cut by 20 GiB (82.8%).
justification: Memory and speed savings measured for FlashLoop vs uncompressed inference on the same pretrained checkpoint.
evidence_quote: To reduce these structural redundancies, we propose FlashLoop, a training-free and loop-native inference framework for pretrained looped Transformers.

claim: Thinking variants are more sensitive to cross-loop compression than base models.
justification: Compression degradation measured per public checkpoint (within_model), then compared across base vs thinking checkpoints trained differently.
evidence_quote: base models tend to be more robust to FlashLoop than their thinking counterparts, suggesting that thinking models may be more sensitive to cross-loop compression.

claim: DAS-Wave reaches 4.00-6.96x mean throughput speedup over paired full-depth AR across four checkpoints and four tasks, the best in all 16 settings.
justification: DAS-Wave vs paired full-depth AR decoding on the same checkpoints in the same inference stack; training-free decoding comparison.
evidence_quote: Across four recurrentmodel checkpoints and mathematics and code workloads, DAS-Wave achieves 4.00–6.96× mean throughput speedup over paired full-depth autoregressive decoding in the same inference stack.

claim: Values mature later than queries and keys across recurrent depth, so full-depth prefix V most improves shallow drafts.
justification: Swaps the recurrent depth of cached prefix K/V channels within the same model and measures draft-target agreement.
evidence_quote: We test the predictive consequence by changing only the recurrent depth of the verified prefix’s cached attention channels.

claim: Mature prefix reads and carried latent states are complementary; either alone gives little or slows decoding (<1x), combined they give 4.11x on Huginn/GSM8K.
justification: Ablation of decoding configurations (prefix reads, carried state) on the same Huginn checkpoint.
evidence_quote: On Huginn/GSM8K, the aligned/no-carry configuration runs at 0.65×; Deep K/V without carry reaches 0.93×, and carry with aligned reads reaches 0.71×, while their combination reaches 4.11× with A = 15.60.

claim: More refinement compute per round increases accepted length but lowers speed; acceptance length is not a sufficient proxy for speedup.
justification: Varies recurrent updates per refinement round in the decoder for the same Huginn model.
evidence_quote: For Huginn, increasing recurrent updates per refinement round from 2 to 8 raises A from 16.49 to 19.56, but reduces speedup from 4.33× to 2.37×.

claim: Lossless under greedy decoding: verification rule unchanged so outputs equal target AR in exact arithmetic.
justification: Theoretical losslessness argument from speculative-decoding verification; not an empirical comparison.
evidence_quote: Because DAS modifies only proposal construction and prefix reads while leaving the target computation and verification rule unchanged, greedy target preservation follows the standard speculative-decoding argument in exact arithmetic

claim: Contrasting early-loop and final-loop logits improves LoopLM reasoning without training and with negligible overhead.
justification: LoopCD is a training-free decoding method compared with greedy and other decoding on the same LoopLM checkpoints.
evidence_quote: We primarily compare our method with greedy decoding, which corresponds to the standard decoding of LoopLMs.

claim: Hard tokens with early overconfidence then revision make up 10-15% of reasoning traces and drive errors.
justification: Descriptive analysis of per-token confidence dynamics across loops; not a model comparison.
evidence_quote: However, a minority subset of tokens exhibits the opposite behavior: the model becomes confident too early and later attempts to revise its initially confident prediction.

claim: An amateur loop at roughly 15-30% of recurrence depth works best.
justification: Sweeps the amateur loop index of LoopCD on the same checkpoints.
evidence_quote: As shown in Table 4, choosing an early loop, roughly 15–30% of the recurrence depth, often works well across tasks and models.

claim: LoopCD combines with early exit: early exit roughly doubles Huginn throughput and LoopCD keeps quality gains on top.
justification: Early exit and LoopCD combined as inference procedures on the same Huginn checkpoint.
evidence_quote: We also combine LoopCD with early exit, which stops recurrence before the final loop when the hidden states change only marginally across consecutive iterations.

claim: Refill CDB achieves 1.32-1.53x throughput over full-depth continuous batching on Ouro (96-99% of the bound); on Huginn no-refill reaches 1.30-1.37x (83-96%).
justification: CDB refill/no-refill vs full-depth continuous batching are serving strategies for the same Ouro and Huginn checkpoints.
evidence_quote: We compare CDB using no-refill and refill against standard token-level CB, which runs rmax loops

claim: FLOP savings from early exit do not automatically reduce wall-clock; in the memory-bound regime shrinking the batch saves little time, which is why refill is needed.
justification: Efficiency analysis of early exit vs full depth on the same checkpoints; FLOP savings vs wall-clock time.
evidence_quote: We find that early exits reduce recurrent-core FLOPs, but fewer FLOPs do not always reduce wall-clock time, especially in the memory bound regime.

claim: Decode-FLOP speedup estimates overestimate end-to-end gains because prefill (3.7-36% of GPU time) is unaffected by early exit.
justification: Analysis of how prefill share limits end-to-end speedup of early exit for the same checkpoints; no architecture comparison.
evidence_quote: Decode FLOPs alone (Sdec ) overestimate end-to-end speedup because depth-adaptive decoding does not reduce prefill latency.

claim: Non-looped boundary layers (prelude/coda, embedding, LM head) slow and complicate adaptive-depth scheduling; fully looped architectures are best suited.
justification: Architectural conclusion drawn from two public checkpoints (Ouro 1.4B, Huginn 3.5B) with different sizes, data, and training.
evidence_quote: Experiments on Ouro 1.4B and Huginn 3.5B show that fully looped architectures are best suited to depth-adaptive inference

claim: Zero-shot single-slot KV sharing collapses Ouro-1.4B on GSM8K (0.23%) but slightly improves Huginn (32.52% vs 30.93%), contradicting Ouro's reported near-lossless sharing.
justification: Zero-shot KV-sharing layouts applied to each public checkpoint at fixed depth versus its full depth-indexed cache.
evidence_quote: Neither model was trained for this setting, so KV sharing is a zero-shot capability here.

claim: Depth-adaptive decoding Pareto-dominates fixed-depth truncation in accuracy vs mean depth; a lookahead gate predicting exit one step early costs no accuracy, but a pre-loop gate fails.
justification: Exit gates (pretrained, lookahead, pre-loop) and fixed-depth truncation compared on the same frozen backbone.
evidence_quote: we train two additional exit gates on the frozen model: a lookahead gate, which predicts the exit one step in advance, and a pre-loop gate, which predicts the exit before the loop starts.

claim: Per-channel INT4 damage in Huginn is localized to the non-residual loop-entry adapter (feedback exposure), not the residual core.
justification: Post-training INT4 applied to different components of the same Huginn checkpoint, compared against its bf16 outputs.
evidence_quote: We first isolate the adapter and recurrent core. Adapter-only INT4 drops final-step agreement with bf16 to 10.5%, whereas quantizing all 16 core projections leaves 87.9% (Figure 1a).

claim: Removing recirculated prior-step error raises agreement from 10.4% to 69.2%, isolating feedback as the cause.
justification: Controlled intervention on recirculated error within the same quantized Huginn rollout.
evidence_quote: To test whether recirculating prior state error drives this damage, we vary how much of that error reaches the adapter at the next step.

claim: One-step GPTQ is worse than round-to-nearest on five of nine looped checkpoints; trajectory-accumulated Hessians beat both on all nine.
justification: GPTQ, RTN, and trajectory calibration are PTQ methods applied to each existing checkpoint; comparisons are per checkpoint.
evidence_quote: Across nine checkpoints from seven looped architectures, onestep GPTQ is worse than round-to-nearest (RTN) on the primary task metric for five checkpoints.

claim: Fully residual looping without adapter (COCONUT) does not compound INT4 error; agreement rises over latent steps.
justification: INT4 COCONUT agreement with its bf16 version tracked across latent steps of the same model.
evidence_quote: On 15 fixed prompts, COCONUT agreement rises from 44.8% after the quantized base forward to 61.5% after 8 latent recurrences.

claim: Real kernel: W4A16 Marlin gives modest 1.21-1.23x batch-1 latency speedup on Huginn with 3.80x smaller shared-projection weights.
justification: Latency of the same Huginn model in bf16 vs W4A16 kernel at batch 1.
evidence_quote: On a single NVIDIA A100 at batch size 1, median eager latency for a 32-step Huginn forward on a 7-token prompt is 303.9 ms in bf16 and 250.9 ms with the Marlin W4A16 kernel (g=128), a 1.21× speedup

claim: Lossless speedup up to 6.83x on Raven (R=32) and up to 3.36x on Ouro (R=4) over standard AR decoding, measured as decode-phase wall-clock.
justification: Training-free self-speculative decoding vs standard AR decoding on the same checkpoints.
evidence_quote: Across various tasks, L OOP S PEC provides consistent speedups over standard autoregressive decoding.

claim: Early recurrent states are good drafters: Raven-Llama-3.2 depth-1 greedy agreement exceeds 86% and passes 99% by depth 8.
justification: Agreement of intermediate recurrent depths with the final depth of the same Raven-Llama model.
evidence_quote: In Looped Transformers, proposals derived from intermediate recurrent states can tightly approximate the target distribution.

claim: Speedups are smaller for long chain-of-thought thinking models and sampling (up to 2.95x greedy, 2.83x sampling).
justification: Speedup measured per checkpoint vs its own AR decoding; smaller-speedup conclusion compares thinking vs base checkpoints trained differently.
evidence_quote: Table 2 reports the performance of L OOP S PEC in reasoning models with the thinking mode enabled.

claim: Accepted length (recurrent-step reduction) overstates wall-clock speedup when prelude/coda are heavy (Raven), since gamma excludes P and C cost.
justification: Explains gap between accepted length and wall-clock speedup across LoopSpec settings on the same models.
evidence_quote: Notably, γ measures the reduction in serial recurrent steps but excludes the cost of P and C computation.

claim: Training-free LoopSpec beats a trained DFlash drafter on Ouro thinking models.
justification: LoopSpec vs trained DFlash drafter are speculative decoding methods for the same Ouro thinking target models.
evidence_quote: We additionally compare our training-free L OOP S PEC to DFlash (Chen et al., 2026) on various reasoning tasks, where DFlash is an effective training-based speculative decoding method

claim: Untrained cache-sharing methods (Huginn-style reuse, Ouro last/average KV) significantly degrade Ouro on long reasoning.
justification: Untrained cache-sharing policies applied to the released Ouro checkpoint versus its default cache.
evidence_quote: our analysis (Appendix B) suggests that directly applying untrained cache-sharing methods to Ouro, including those proposed by Geiping et al. [12] and Zhu et al. [1], significantly degrades performance on long reasoning tasks.

claim: Memory saving trades against batch-1 speed: MELT decodes slower than Ouro at batch 1 but fits a larger batch.
justification: MELT-1.6B (fine-tuned Ouro derivative with extra parameters) vs public Ouro-1.4B-Thinking; parameters and training differ.
evidence_quote: Table 10: Inference efficiency metrics for MELT-1.6B, Ouro-1.4B-Thinking, and Qwen3-1.7B.

claim: Training with sequential KV dynamics is essential: replacing chunk-wise training with parallel SFT nearly halves capability.
justification: Component-removal ablation retrains the same MELT model on the same data after each removal.
evidence_quote: Starting from the full model, we progressively remove elements of the training procedure one by one, following their order of introduction, and fully retrain the model after each removal to ensure a fair comparison.

claim: At matched 4x cache budget, compressing the loop axis preserves GSM8K (0.800 vs teacher 0.794) while final-loop reuse collapses to 0.000 and head/layer/precision baselines lose more.
justification: Cache codecs and baselines swapped onto the same frozen Ouro teacher at the same cache budget; recurrence and attention unchanged.
evidence_quote: Our experiments separate these by only changing what the cache stores while the teacher is kept frozen and the attention pattern and recurrence intact.

claim: The loop axis is the most compressible KV axis, and this transfers to Huginn where an SVD codec is near-lossless to 32x.
justification: SVD codec applied to frozen Huginn KV cache and compared with the uncompressed teacher.
evidence_quote: Huginn-3.5B, where an SVD codec remains near-lossless to 32× compression in decoderindependent evaluation.

claim: Memory reduction translates into batch capacity, not decode speed: latent-store path is compute-bound in the current kernel.
justification: Serving capacity and latency of LLA vs teacher full cache on the same Ouro checkpoints.
evidence_quote: The latent-store path caches only the latent and realizes the ρ× saving; because the current kernel reconstructs cached tokens on read, it is compute-bound (108 versus 748 peak tokens/s at the reported endpoints).

claim: Teacher-forced codec fitting suffers exposure bias in long rollouts; on-policy refinement fixes much of it at 3-5x compression.
justification: On-policy vs off-policy codec fitting on the same frozen teacher; only codec parameters change, backbone fixed.
evidence_quote: The swapped model samples completions, the frozen teacher scores those sampled prefixes, and only codec parameters are updated.

claim: Long-context retrieval bounds usable compression: reliable passkey retrieval >=64k at <=5.33x, 16k at 10.67x, 8k at 14.2x.
justification: Passkey retrieval of the same frozen backbone under increasing codec compression ratios.
evidence_quote: the reliable-retrieval length (longest context with retrieval ≥ 0.9) shrinks steeply as compression rises: ≥64k at ≤ 5.33×, 16k at 10.67×, 8k at 14.2×.

claim: Under W4A4, LoopQ improves mean downstream accuracy by 68.8% (relative) and reduces perplexity by 87.7% vs the strongest static PTQ baseline.
justification: LoopQ vs static PTQ baselines are post-training quantization methods applied to the same pretrained LoopLM checkpoints.
evidence_quote: LoopQ, a loop-aware post-training quantization framework that preserves a shared quantized backbone while introducing lightweight loop-dependent adaptations

claim: Quantization error grows across recursion with spikes at loop transitions, and can be multiplicatively amplified when the loop map has Lipschitz factor above 1.
justification: Theoretical amplification argument (Propositions 1-2) plus qualitative description of error growth; not a model comparison.
evidence_quote: Proposition 2 then implies that errors can be multiplicatively amplified across loops rather than merely accumulate linearly.

claim: Long-context prediction (LAMBADA) is most sensitive to cross-loop error accumulation.
justification: Inference from per-task gains of PTQ methods applied to the same checkpoints (LoopFormer, Parcae, Ouro).
evidence_quote: This shows that long-context prediction is especially sensitive to accumulated cross-loop distortion.

claim: WFD gives 2.42x (Ouro-2.6B) and 3.54x (Huginn-3.5B) end-to-end throughput over AR, 1.27x over draft-then-verify, lossless under greedy without KV sharing.
justification: WFD vs AR vs draft-then-verify are training-free decoding schedules on the same Ouro and Huginn checkpoints.
evidence_quote: To address the issue, we introduce Wavefront Decoding (WFD), a training-free self-speculative decoding framework designed for looped language models.

claim: Speedup comes from converting serial recurrent calls into batched calls, not from reducing FLOPs.
justification: Mechanistic explanation (memory-bandwidth-bound batched recurrent calls); not a matched empirical comparison.
evidence_quote: Instead, it converts serial applications of R into batched applications. In the decoding regime, R, which consists of a stack of transformer layers, is memory-bandwidth bound.

claim: Cross-recurrence KV sharing raises Huginn WFD speedup to 4.81x (GSM8K) while staying within 0.70 points of AR under the same sharing; Ouro cannot use naive post-hoc sharing.
justification: Inference-time KV sharing applied to the same Huginn checkpoint, compared with AR under the same sharing; Ouro post-hoc sharing tested likewise.
evidence_quote: Huginn has been shown to tolerate inferencetime KV sharing without additional training (Geiping et al., 2026).

claim: Speedups of WFD and draft-then-verify decrease monotonically with user batch size.
justification: Speedups of decoding schedules across batch sizes on the same checkpoints.
evidence_quote: Figure 5 shows this trend; the speedups of both WFD and DtV decrease monotonically with b on both models.

claim: Contrasting with an earlier recurrent state improves reasoning and code at full depth across four looped families.
justification: Training-free contrastive decoding vs unguided decoding on the same public looped checkpoints.
evidence_quote: We introduce LoopCD, a training-free contrastive decoding framework that guides token selection by contrasting the final prediction with an earlier recurrent pass

claim: Halving depth costs 0.17-1.29 points unguided; LoopCD at half depth adds 0.75-1.29 points, closing the gap in all six settings.
justification: Same checkpoints evaluated at full vs half recurrent depth, with and without LoopCD guidance.
evidence_quote: Reducing recurrent iterations by half incurs an accuracy penalty of 0.17 to 1.29 points on the unguided seven-benchmark multiple-choice mean.

claim: Guidance gain scales with the reference's disagreement with the final prediction rather than its standalone accuracy; first iteration is the best logit reference (Huginn hidden-state reference peaks later).
justification: Varies which earlier iteration serves as contrastive reference for the same checkpoint.
evidence_quote: The empirical results demonstrate that guidance gain scales reliably with the reference’s disagreement from the final prediction, rather than its standalone competence.

claim: Routing-related quantities stabilize earlier than representation-related quantities across recurrent depth.
justification: Descriptive analysis of when attention routing vs representations stabilize across depth within Huginn; not a comparison of models.
evidence_quote: routing-related quantities, including attention support and attention distributions, stabilize substantially earlier than representation-related quantities such as hidden states and attention outputs.

claim: Support reuse yields attention speedups growing with context, 1.15x at 512 to 1.76x at 4K (late-reuse, attention only); whole 32-step attention trajectory 1.36x at 4K.
justification: WISE support reuse vs native FlashAttention timed on the same Huginn attention geometry; training-free.
evidence_quote: we introduce WISE (Working-set Inference with Support Exploitation), a training-free method that uses unrestricted global attention during early recurrent steps

claim: Quality is preserved through 2K context but drops 3.3 F1 points at 4K.
justification: Quality of WISE vs native attention on the same Huginn model across context lengths.
evidence_quote: comparisons show no detected average F1 loss through 2K, while a 3.3-point reduction emerges at 4K.

claim: Truncating recurrence at the discovery depth hurts, so late representation refinement still matters even after routing has stabilized.
justification: Truncated recurrence at discovery depth vs full recurrence on the same model.
evidence_quote: Truncating recurrence at the discovery depth worsens teacher-forced gold-answer loss, indicating that representation refinement remains useful after global routing has largely stabilized.

claim: Early shared-layer predictions are mostly correct: only 13-17% (2x6) or 6-14% (4x3) need correction after the first group.
justification: Profiles prediction flips between early and later layers of the same parameter-shared model during inference.
evidence_quote: In order to assess the accuracy of the predictions made from our network at earlier layers, we profiled the proportion of predictions that were flipped between pairs of layers during inference.

claim: Gains shrink for short generations because pipeline fill/drain is not overlapped.
justification: Discussion of a runtime limitation (pipeline fill/drain) of SPEED; not a matched comparison.
evidence_quote: One factor is the generation length, as the first iterations and final iterations in pipelined decoding aren’t completely overlapped (as discussed in Appendix D.2).

claim: Reducing iterations 24 -> 20 with larger step sizes is nearly free; 16 is acceptable; 12 collapses GPT-2 with step size 1 pretraining.
justification: Same PSPLM pretrained with step size 1 evaluated with fewer iterations and larger inference step sizes.
evidence_quote: Table 1: Inference performance of PSPLMs pre-trained with step size 1. Values in parentheses indicates relative change from non-reduced iteration counts.

claim: Speedup is wall-clock and roughly linear in reduced iterations (no added computation).
justification: Wall-clock speedup of the same model at reduced vs full iteration counts.
evidence_quote: Values in parentheses indicates relative change from non-reduced iteration counts. Speed reflects the acceleration of the forward pass wallclock time.

claim: A compressed looped model that works at its default depth keeps working as it loops longer; error accumulation holds only for loops that never settle.
justification: Post-training quantized vs full-precision versions of the same trained models evaluated at default and longer loop counts.
evidence_quote: We quantize weights after training by round-to-nearest, with one scale per tensor (t), per output channel (c) or per group of 32 input weights (g32)

claim: Collapse needs no accumulating bias: zero-mean fresh noise produces the same accuracy cliff; size of the error sets the cliff, fixedness decides whether more loops repair it.
justification: Noise injected at inference into the same trained TRM, varying noise size and fixedness.
evidence_quote: Zero-mean noise drawn anew at every call has no bias to build up. Injected into TRM Sudoku-MLP, it still takes the model from 62.9% to 2.3% as its size grows

claim: Collapsed models still settle; 8-bit finishing loops recover them.
justification: Collapsed quantized model handed to precise or 8-bit finishing loops; same trained weights, different inference precision.
evidence_quote: We hand the settled state of each collapsed model to a precise loop for a few finishing steps.

claim: Huginn and Recurrent-OLMo-2 settle and recover with precise final loops; Ouro does not settle and loses accuracy with extra loops even at full precision.
justification: Each public checkpoint evaluated at extra loops and precisions; settling contrast is across families trained differently (Ouro trained for four loops).
evidence_quote: Ouro is trained for four loops, and even at full precision its accuracy falls when it loops longer.

claim: Halting-head stopping plus 8-bit finishing beats fixed-depth inference at lower modelled weight traffic.
justification: Halting-head stopping plus 8-bit finishing vs fixed-depth inference on the same trained puzzle models.
evidence_quote: From these findings we build a controller that stops a puzzle when the model’s halting head fires and then takes a few 8-bit finishing steps.

claim: Recall is what prevents overthinking; recalled models appear to converge to a fixed point rather than becoming unstable as iterations grow.
justification: DT vs DT-Recall trained with consistent width and iterations on same data (recall adds input channels); stability assessed across test-time iterations.
evidence_quote: However, to provide a fair comparison, we use consistent values for these parameters across our experiments since we find that all architectures benefit from additional width and depth.

claim: Random starting iteration n in progressive training matters: n=0 gives 90.27% vs 97.12% with random n on 512-bit prefix sums.
justification: Same DT-Recall architecture and data; only the progressive-loss starting iteration sampling changes.
evidence_quote: we modify the algorithm slightly, to always use n = 0, rather than randomly choosing that value.

claim: The variance is traced to the spurious correlation between sequence length and number of loops; randomizing loop count during training reduces OOD variance and stabilizes predictions across inference-time loop counts.
justification: Looped models with deterministic vs randomized loop-count training share architecture and the 100k-step recipe; only the stopping schedule changes.
evidence_quote: All models are trained with AdamW using batch size 64 for 100k gradient steps.

claim: Stochastic schedules stabilize rather than monotonically improve accuracy: OOD accuracy improves from deterministic to +-5 window but decreases at +-10.
justification: Stochastic window sizes compared on the same looped architecture with identical training recipe.
evidence_quote: All models are trained with AdamW using batch size 64 for 100k gradient steps.

claim: RL-Halting gives best OOD accuracy and lowest std on three of four tasks, but on Copy it stabilizes a worse computation.
justification: RL-Halting vs hand-designed schedules use the same 100k-step recipe and tasks; RL-Halting adds a lightweight stopping head.
evidence_quote: All models are trained with AdamW using batch size 64 for 100k gradient steps.

claim: Continuous latent recurrence degrades with more recurrent depth because noise accumulates and representations drift; discretizing and re-embedding between iterations anchors states and fixes this.
justification: Continuous vs discrete latent supervision are ablations trained on the same graph task distribution; parameter equality not stated.
evidence_quote: Figure 4 depicts the OOD generalization performance of our methods, ablating across the ingredients described above

claim: The stability recipe does not change mean accuracy but removes seed sensitivity: the ablated model's graph OOD swings from 62 to 76 across seeds versus 0.2 variation.
justification: Ablation removing LayerScale and gate on the same tasks with 3-seed protocol; removed components change parameters slightly.
evidence_quote: The last row ablates our stability recipe (no LayerScale, no gate).

claim: DT-L learns algorithms that extrapolate to harder problems with fewer parameters and more reliability than DT, and learns TSP where DT fails.
justification: Fulltext not available locally; baseline setup for DT vs DT-L cannot be verified.

claim: The best block position depends on task category: 7-4*2-5 is best for math, while an earlier block (3-4*2-9) is best for reading comprehension.
justification: Block position varied with fixed 4-layer block looped twice in the same 16-layer model and same mid-training data, so layer calls are equal.
evidence_quote: To further examine the impact of recursive layer choice, we fix the recursive “thinking” block size and vary its starting position from layer 2 to 12 in steps of 2

claim: For direct LM-head supervision, reading only the post-loop latents beats supervising every iteration; the auxiliary-decoder variant prefers per-iteration readout.
justification: Latent-supervision readout variants compared with backbone, K, R, c, and answer loss held fixed.
evidence_quote: We compare it against five alternatives, holding the rest fixed

claim: Trained loop depth matters strongly and extra test-time loops beyond the trained depth do not help.
justification: Separately trained models with different R share K, c, and data; inference-time R sweep reuses the R=6 model.
evidence_quote: We train separate models for R P t2, . . . , 6u, fixing K“6 and c“25 so that the latent prefix has Kc “ 150 positions and only the depth of sequential refinement changes (Table 5).

claim: The looped padded backbone helps even without latent supervision, and gold-CoT supervision adds further gains.
justification: Looped backbone without latent supervision vs CODI + SIM-CoT on the same Llama backbone, all trained on GSM8k-Aug.
evidence_quote: All methods are trained on GSM8k-Aug [Deng et al., 2023].

claim: A 6.01M-parameter LoRA retrofit over frozen base weights matches the 180.6M full-block retrofit overall (identical protocol), better in-support, worse beyond depth 11.
justification: LoRA adapter and full-block retrofits use the identical surgery and training regimen; trained parameter counts differ (6.01M vs 180.6M).
evidence_quote: The installation half of that claim now holds at two budgets, the same regimen installing the procedure through a 6M adapter over frozen weights (Section 6.2).

claim: Random deep supervision with per-step detachment beats truncated BPTT: TBPTT costs more and plateaus at higher LM loss; removing the selective gate also gives higher loss.
justification: Component ablations of LoopUS over the same 5000-step training curves; TBPTT vs deep supervision share architecture (gate removal drops few parameters).
evidence_quote: Figure 9 analyzes how LLM changes when key components of LoopUS are removed or replaced.

claim: Which layers are looped barely matters: early, middle and output-side 5-layer intervals are within 0.19 point; full-decoder recurrence is only 0.27 point better at 2.51x the layer calls.
justification: Only the recurrent interval changes; source model, modules, data, and update budget fixed. Full-decoder recurrence uses 2.51x layer calls.
evidence_quote: Table 2 varies only the interval at fixed K = 6; the source, interface, transition modules, curriculum, data, update budget, and continuation seeds remain fixed.

claim: Recurrence contributes only a small gain over the same checkpoint run with K=0 (boundary only).
justification: Same Penelope checkpoints run with K=0 at inference vs validation-selected recurrent depth.
evidence_quote: As a mechanism diagnostic, inference-only K = 0 isolates the contextualized boundary from recurrent refinement.

claim: Uniform per-loop supervision (same hard labels or same 7B teacher at every iteration) stagnates or regresses with more iterations; reversing teacher order collapses at iteration 3.
justification: Recursive supervision variants share the same architecture and training data; only per-iteration supervision differs.
evidence_quote: All recursive variants share the same architecture based on simple layer stacking, ensuring that differences arise solely from how supervision is applied across iterations.

claim: Naive state-integration choices (init injection, additive, concat-project, gate, AdaLN modulation) degrade with more iterations when retrofitting; only cross-attention stays flat.
justification: Retrospective integration variants fine-tuned in the same setup; fusion modules differ in parameters.
evidence_quote: To evaluate the impact of retrospective reasoning design, we compare our cross-attention approach (XAttn) with five common alternatives
