claim: Without the carry constraint, gradient descent drives the carry above 1 at higher learning rates and the hidden state explodes; the coda LayerNorm keeps loss finite so loss curves can hide the failure.
justification: Constrained vs unconstrained carry trained on Tiny Shakespeare with same d, T, and 120 steps across learning rates.
evidence_quote: against an unconstrained free scalar carry across learning rates on Tiny Shakespeare (d = 24, T = 8, 120 steps).

claim: On cross-channel tasks gradient descent stores depth-memory in the nonlinear block and leaves the constrained carry at rest; the carry is recruited only on axis-aligned per-channel tasks.
justification: Mechanistic finding about where trained toy models store depth memory; not a matched model comparison.
evidence_quote: Training experiments across six tasks, including a controlled ablation, reveal that the linear carry is not the depth-memory mechanism

claim: Looped-LM training instability at high loop counts has two components: early gradient oscillation and residual-state explosion; per-layer RMSNorm alone does not prevent the explosion.
justification: LT models with 6, 9, 12 loops and FLT control share the 6-layer backbone and the same pretraining setup in the diagnostic window.
evidence_quote: In Figure 2, we compare LT models with 6, 9, and 12 loop iterations using the same 6-layer Transformer backbone, and include a 12-loop Fully Looped Transformer (FLT) as a stable control.

claim: Fully looped connectivity with plain residual fusion only attenuates residual explosion; attention-based injection is needed for stable training.
justification: FLT variants (residual vs attention injection) and LT ablated under the same Section 3 settings; parameter equality across injection variants not stated.
evidence_quote: In the ablation experiment, We check the stability of different methods using the same settings as Section 3.

claim: Models trained with fixed loops benefit from more test-time loops only within the training range; beyond it performance fluctuates.
justification: Models pretrained at fixed loop counts evaluated at different inference loop counts.
evidence_quote: For models pretrained with 3, 6, 9, and 12 loop iterations, we evaluated their performance at 1, 3, 6, 9, and 12 loop iterations, as shown in Figure 5.

claim: Standard 1/sqrt(depth) residual scaling fails for looped networks because shared weights make residual updates correlated; 1/N scaling is required to keep the residual stream bounded.
justification: Primarily a theoretical scaling result; supporting experiments compare residual scalings on the same looped architecture.
evidence_quote: We show that this is insufficient for looped architectures: weight sharing makes residual updates correlated across iterations, requiring the stronger scaling ε = 1/N .

claim: Prelude/coda layers (Huginn-style) do not change the stability tendencies of the recurrence.
justification: Toy looped models with and without prelude/coda trained on the same 4-digit addition data; prelude/coda add parameters.
evidence_quote: The models are trained on 4-digit by 4-digit addition problems (e.g., “1234 + 5678 = 6912”) using a vocabulary consisting of digits, arithmetic operators, and special tokens.

claim: Random loop sampling improves performance retention beyond the training loop count but does not fix effective stability and is sensitive to the sampling range; L2 regularization between consecutive states adds almost nothing.
justification: Fixed vs randomly sampled training loop counts (and L2 regularizer) on the same toy architecture and 100k-sample addition data.
evidence_quote: The training dataset comprises 100,000 samples which are randomly generated, a scale sufficient to preclude rote memorization and compel the model to learn a generalized addition algorithm.

claim: Residual scaling by running depth (1/((t-1)L+l)) shrinks later-iteration updates so much that their gradient contribution vanishes; a fixed 1/T factor is used instead.
justification: Design rationale citing an unreported empirical finding; no setup or comparison numbers given.
evidence_quote: yields tiny factors for later iterations of deep unrollings, which we found empirically neutralizes their gradient contribution.

claim: Weight tying changes residual scaling: the conservative aligned regime needs exponent p=1/2 rather than DeepNorm's 1/4 as loop count grows at fixed physical depth.
justification: Theoretical perturbation bound on residual scaling exponents for tied depth.
evidence_quote: The bound recovers the DeepNorm exponent when visits decorrelate, but in the conservative aligned regime it requires the exponent to increase from 1/4 to 1/2 as loop count grows at fixed physical depth.

claim: Truncating gradients to the last outer cycle (HRM) puts the truncated module in the untied-DeepNorm regime; analysis counts only gradient-visible visits.
justification: Theoretical analysis of gradient-truncated HRM modules.
evidence_quote: The truncation thus places H in the untied-DeepNorm regime even though H is

claim: A training-time penalty on fluctuation exceeding progress (co-design SFT) reduces late-stage loss variability and improves held-out accuracy at matched training loss.
justification: Paired SFT from the same TRM checkpoint with identical data order, hyperparameters, architecture, and seed; only the co-design penalty differs.
evidence_quote: Task-only SFT and P/S co-design use identical data order, optimization hyperparameters, architecture, and random seed, as summarized in Table 6.

claim: With all four loops active, a standard shared LoRA update is much more effective at later loop positions than earlier ones.
justification: Same trained LoRA adapter activated at one loop position at a time on the frozen Ouro backbone.
evidence_quote: Figure 1a evaluates a trained adapter at each loop position in turn, with the adapter active only at that position and the backbone running all four loops.

claim: Dense supervision trains exits; scale control needs a scale-visible loss or removing scale from the loop (inter-loop normalization).
justification: Readout, penalty, and normalization variants are controlled ablations of the same 44M/129M looped stacks trained on WikiText-103.
evidence_quote: We train autoregressive looped transformers on WikiText-103 [Merity et al., 2017] with K = 4 recurrent applications of a shared decoder stack.

claim: At 1.4B Ouro-scale with inter-loop RMSNorm, both checkpoints are essentially K-invariant after ~1.3B tokens, consistent with inter-loop norm bounding scale.
justification: Each 1.4B checkpoint evaluated at K = 2, 3, 4; K-invariance is a same-model inference comparison.
evidence_quote: Both checkpoints are essentially K-invariant on this slice (CE varies by less than 0.01 nats across K=2,3,4)

claim: SHIFT (single-pass first, then looped) reaches comparable final performance to pure looped training with less training time; the switch point matters (too early suboptimal, too late fails to converge).
justification: SHIFT and pure looped training use the same shared block on the same Markov dataset; only the schedule of single-pass vs looped training differs.
evidence_quote: Training is transitioned to Looped-Attn when Single-Attn reaches loss plateaus.

claim: Forcing more loops does not monotonically help: forced-depth accuracy can drop for medium and hard tokens, because later loops are not trained to refine monotonically.
justification: Same LoopRPT and baseline checkpoints evaluated at forced latent depths with exit threshold 1.0.
evidence_quote: We set the exit threshold to 1.0 and vary the latent steps to evaluate performance under compulsory computation.

claim: With more recurrence steps (16 to 32), LTO's gain shrinks because random-init trajectories become less diverse, leaving fewer problems with mixed correct and incorrect samples.
justification: LTO is test-time latent optimization on the same Huginn base model, compared at different thinking-step counts.
evidence_quote: From the experimental results in Table A3, we can see that LTO achieves a consistent improvement over the base model in all the cases

claim: Without Ouro's staged schedule the exit gate collapses to exit-after-loop-1; LR warmup prevents the early collapse and a larger KL/entropy coefficient beta lets the gate recover; LM loss does not reveal the collapse.
justification: Warmup and beta sweep runs share architecture and the main 2M-token-batch configuration.
evidence_quote: All runs use the same 2M-token-batch configuration as the main recipe (Table 1).

claim: Normalization placement around the shared block matters: post-norm and sandwich-norm fail to train because gradients vanish through the block; a final norm before the LM head removes loss spikes.
justification: Normalization variants share architecture, optimizer, T=4, batch, and a matched 19K-step budget.
evidence_quote: Unless stated otherwise, all runs use the architecture and optimizer of our main recipe, T =4, a 500K-token batch, and a matched budget of 19K steps.

claim: RL (RLTT) on the LoopLM helps only when rollout solve rate gives mixed-success groups and the LR is large enough to move the policy.
justification: Conclusion drawn from two RL runs that differ in starting checkpoint, task (MATH vs GSM8K), and solve rate.
evidence_quote: A mid-trained checkpoint of an earlier run of this recipe already solved about three quarters of its MATH rollouts, and RLTT left MATH unchanged

claim: Think-at-Hard (2511.08577) could not be reproduced on this training mixture: repeated-step loss never fell below first-step loss.
justification: Repeated-step vs first-step loss within the authors' reproduction; failure judged against gains published by the original TaH paper.
evidence_quote: In our reproduction, the repeated-step LM loss never fell below the first-step loss, and accuracy degraded substantially on several downstream benchmarks.

claim: Muon is more stable than AdamW (including Huginn's AdamW variant) for recurrent training; AdamW loss spikes to NaN.
justification: Optimizer comparison on the same recurrent TinyLlama model with the same data order.
evidence_quote: Loss vs. step for multiple training runs on the same data order with different optimizers, using a learning rate of 5e−5 for AdamW and 0.001 for Muon.

claim: Which layers to keep: early layers as prelude and later layers as recurrent block and coda, dropping middle layers; this beats ShortGPT-selected layers.
justification: Layer-selection variants from Llama-1b keep the same recurrent shape and train on the same Fineweb-Edu data.
evidence_quote: We measure the training loss on Fineweb-Edu with different layer selections from Llama-1b.
